Global weak solutions for the three-dimensional chemotaxis-Navier-Stokes system with nonlinear diffusionThanks: Supported in part by National Natural Science Foundation of China (No. 11171063).

Qingshan Zhang Address: Department of Mathematics, Southeast University, Nanjing 211189, P. R. China Email address: qingshan11@yeah.net and Yuxiang Li Address: Department of Mathematics, Southeast University, Nanjing 211189, P. R. China Email address: lieyx@seu.edu.cn
Abstract.

We consider an initial-boundary value problem for the incompressible chemotaxis-Navier-Stokes equations generalizing the porous-medium-type diffusion model

{nt+u⋅∇n=Δnm−∇⋅(nχ(c)∇c),x∈Ω,t>0,ct+u⋅∇c=Δ​c−n​f​(c),x∈Ω,t>0,ut+κ(u⋅∇)u=Δu+∇P+n∇Φ,x∈Ω,t>0,∇⋅u=0,x∈Ω,t>0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}\vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptn_{t}+u\cdot\nabla n=\Delta n^{m}-\nabla\cdot(n\chi(c)\nabla c),&{}x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptc_{t}+u\cdot\nabla c=\Delta c-nf(c),&{}x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptu_{t}+\kappa(u\cdot\nabla)u=\Delta u+\nabla P+n\nabla\Phi,&{}x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0pt\nabla\cdot u=0,&{}x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\end{array}\right.

in a bounded convex domain Ω⊂ℝ3\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}. It is proved that if m≥23m\geq\frac{2}{3}, κ∈ℝ\kappa\in\mathbb{R}, 0<χ∈C2​([0,∞))0<\chi\in C^{2}([0,\infty)), 0≤f∈C1​([0,∞))0\leq f\in C^{1}([0,\infty)) with f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0 and Φ∈W1,∞​(Ω)\Phi\in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega), then for sufficiently smooth initial data (n0,c0,u0)(n_{0},c_{0},u_{0}) the model possesses at least one global weak solution.

Key words and phrases: 
chemotaxis, Navier-Stokes equation, nonlinear diffusion, global existence.
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
35Q92, 35K55, 35Q35, 76S05, 92C17.

1. Introduction

Chemotaxis is the directed movement of living cells under the effects of chemical gradients. Aerobic bacteria such as Bacillus subtilis often live in thin fluid layers near solid-air-water contact line, in which the swimming bacteria move towards higher concentration of oxygen according to mechanism of chemotaxis and meanwhile the movement of fluid is under the influence of gravitational force generated by bacteria themselves. Both the oxygen concentration and bacteria density are transported by the fluid and diffuse through the fluid ([5, 20, 14]).

To model such biological processes, Tuval et al. [22] proposed the following model

{nt+u⋅∇n=Δn−∇⋅(nχ(c)∇c),x∈Ω,t>0,ct+u⋅∇c=Δ​c−n​f​(c),x∈Ω,t>0,ut+κ(u⋅∇)u=Δu+∇P+n∇Φ,x∈Ω,t>0,∇⋅u=0,x∈Ω,t>0\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}\vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptn_{t}+u\cdot\nabla n=\Delta n-\nabla\cdot(n\chi(c)\nabla c),&{}x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptc_{t}+u\cdot\nabla c=\Delta c-nf(c),&{}x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptu_{t}+\kappa(u\cdot\nabla)u=\Delta u+\nabla P+n\nabla\Phi,&{}x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0pt\nabla\cdot u=0,&{}x\in\Omega,\ t>0\end{array}\right.

in a domain Ω⊂ℝN\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{N}, where the scalar functions n=n⁡(x,t)n=n(x,t) and c=c⁡(x,t)c=c(x,t) denote bacterial density and the concentration of oxygen, respectively. The vector u=(u1​(x,t),u2​(x,t),⋯,uN​(x,t))u=(u_{1}(x,t),u_{2}(x,t),\cdots,u_{N}(x,t)) is the fluid velocity field and the associated pressure is represented by P=P⁡(x,t)P=P(x,t). The function χ\chi is called the chemotactic sensitivity, ff is the consumption rate oxygen by the bacteria and κ∈ℝ\kappa\in\mathbb{R} measures the strength of nonlinear fluid convection. The given function Φ\Phi stands for the gravitational potential produced by the action of physical forces on the cell.

The chemotaxis fluid system has been studied in the last few years and the main focus is on the solvability result. Under the assumption that χ⁡(c)=χ\chi(c)=\chi is a constant and ff is monotonically increasing with f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0, Lorz [14] constructed local weak solutions in a bounded domain ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N} (N=2,3)(N=2,3) with no-flux boundary condition and in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} in the case of inhomogeneous Dirichlet conditions for oxygen. In bounded convex domains Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}, Winkler [28] proved that the initial-boundary value problem for (1) possesses a unique global classical solution. In [30] the same author showed that the global classical solutions obtained in [28] stabilize to the spatially uniform equilibrium (n¯0,0,0)(\bar{n}_{0},0,0) with n¯0:=1|Ω|​∫Ωn0​(x)​𝑑x\bar{n}_{0}:=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\int_{\Omega}n_{0}(x)dx as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty. Zhang and Li [32] proved that such solution converges to the equilibrium (n¯0,0,0)(\bar{n}_{0},0,0) exponentially in time. By deriving a new type of entropy-energy estimate, Jiang et al. [11] generalized the result of [30] to general bounded domains. For the well-posedness of the Cauchy problem to (1) in the whole space we refer the reader to [6, 13, 2, 31, 34, 3].

When the nonlinear convective term is ignored (κ=0\kappa=0 in (1)), which means the fluid motion is slow, and the model is simplified to the chemotaxis-Stokes equation. In this modified version, global weak solutions are constructed for the two-dimensional Cauchy problem [6]. In a bounded convex domain Ω⊂ℝ3\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}, the chemotaxis-Stokes system possesses at least one global weak solution [28].

The diffusion of bacteria may depend nonlinearly on their densities [9, 23, 20, 19]. Introducing this into the model (1) leads to the chemotaxis-Navier-Stokes system with nonlinear diffusion[4]

{nt+u⋅∇n=∇⋅(D(n)∇n)−∇⋅(nχ(c)∇c),x∈Ω,t>0,ct+u⋅∇c=Δ​c−n​f​(c),x∈Ω,t>0,ut+κ(u⋅∇)u=Δu+∇P+n∇Φ,x∈Ω,t>0,∇⋅u=0,x∈Ω,t>0.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}\vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptn_{t}+u\cdot\nabla n=\nabla\cdot\left(D(n)\nabla n\right)-\nabla\cdot(n\chi(c)\nabla c),&{}x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptc_{t}+u\cdot\nabla c=\Delta c-nf(c),&{}x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptu_{t}+\kappa(u\cdot\nabla)u=\Delta u+\nabla P+n\nabla\Phi,&{}x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0pt\nabla\cdot u=0,&{}x\in\Omega,\ t>0.\end{array}\right.

Up to now, the main issue of investigation to (1) seems to concentrate on the chemotaxis-Stokes variant. Under the assumption D⁡(n)=m​nm−1D(n)=mn^{m-1}, Di Francesco et al. [4] proved that when m∈(32,2]m\in(\frac{3}{2},2] the chemotaxis-Stokes system admits a global-in-time solution for general initial data in the bounded domain Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}. The same result holds in three-dimensional setting under the constraint m∈(7+21712,2]m\in(\frac{7+\sqrt{217}}{12},2]. Tao and Winkler [19, 20] extended the global existence result so as to cover the whole range m∈(1,∞)m\in(1,\infty) in the bounded domain Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} and m∈(87,∞)m\in(\frac{8}{7},\infty) in the bounded convex domain Ω⊂ℝ3\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}. In [13], global existence of weak solution to the Cauchy problem of chemotaxis-Stokes system is established with m=43m=\frac{4}{3} in Ω=ℝ2\Omega=\mathbb{R}^{2}. Recently, Duan and Xiang [7] generalized the global existence result for all exponents m∈[1,∞)m\in[1,\infty) .

In contrast to the chemotaxis-Stokes system, very few results of global solvability are available for the full nonlinear chemotaxis-Navier-Stokes system. In the case Ω⫅ℝ2\Omega\subseteqq\mathbb{R}^{2}, global weak solutions are constructed by setting D⁡(n)=m​nm−1D(n)=mn^{m-1} with m∈[1,∞)m\in[1,\infty) [7]. For the three-dimensional initial-boundary value problem, the only result we are aware of is that when m>43m>\frac{4}{3} the full system with nonlinear diffusion admits a global weak solution provided that Φ∈Ll​o​c1​((0,∞),Ll​o​c1​(Ω))\Phi\in L^{1}_{loc}((0,\infty);L^{1}_{loc}(\Omega)) with ∇Φ∈Ll​o​c2​((0,∞),L∞​(Ω))\nabla\Phi\in L^{2}_{loc}((0,\infty);L^{\infty}(\Omega)), and χ\chi and ff are continuous differentiable satisfying χ′≥0\chi^{\prime}\geq 0, f≥0f\geq 0 and f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0 [24].

Recently, for sufficiently smooth initial data (n0,c0,u0)(n_{0},c_{0},u_{0}), Winkler [29] established global weak solutions of (1) in bounded convex domains Ω⊂ℝ3\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{3} under the assumptions χ∈C2​([0,∞))\chi\in C^{2}([0,\infty)), f∈C1​([0,∞))f\in C^{1}([0,\infty)) with f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0 and Φ∈W1,∞​(Ω)\Phi\in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega). Motivated by the work of [29], our purpose of the present paper is to consider the full chemotaxis-Navier-Stokes system with nonlinear diffusion. In order to formulate our result, we specify the precise mathematical setting: we shall subsequently consider (1) along with boundary conditions

(1.11) D⁡(n)​∂n∂ν=∂c∂ν=0,u=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0D(n)\frac{\partial n}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial c}{\partial\nu}=0,\quad u=0,\quad x\in\partial\Omega,\ t>0

and the initial conditions

(1.12) n⁡(x,0)=n0​(x),c⁡(x,0)=c0​(x),u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x),x∈Ωn(x,0)=n_{0}(x),\quad c(x,0)=c_{0}(x),\quad u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),\quad x\in\Omega

in a bounded convex domains Ω⊂ℝ3\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{3} with smooth boundary, where we assume

{n0∈L​log⁡L⁡(Ω)​is positive,c0∈L∞​(Ω)​is nonnegative and such that​c0∈W1,2​(Ω),u0∈Lσ2​(Ω).\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}\vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptn_{0}\in L\log L(\Omega)\ \mbox{is positive},\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptc_{0}\in L^{\infty}(\Omega)\ \mbox{is nonnegative and such that}\ \sqrt{c_{0}}\in W^{1,2}(\Omega),\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptu_{0}\in L_{\sigma}^{2}(\Omega).\end{array}\right.

With respect to the parameter function in (1), we shall suppose throughout the paper that

(1.17) D⁡(s)∈Cl​o​c1+γ​((0,∞))for some​γ>0,D(s)\in C_{loc}^{1+\gamma}\left((0,\infty)\right)\quad\mbox{for some}\ \gamma>0,
(1.18) D1​sm−1≤D⁡(s)≤D2​sm−1for all​s>0D_{1}s^{m-1}\leq D(s)\leq D_{2}s^{m-1}\quad\mbox{for all}\ s>0

with m≥23m\geq\frac{2}{3} and D2≥D1>0D_{2}\geq D_{1}>0, and that

{χ∈C2([0,∞)),χ>0in[0,∞),f∈C1([0,∞)),f(0)=0,f>0in(0,∞),Φ∈W1,∞​(Ω).\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}\vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0pt\chi\in C^{2}([0,\infty)),\quad\chi>0\quad\mbox{in}\ [0,\infty),\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptf\in C^{1}([0,\infty)),\quad f(0)=0,\quad f>0\quad\mbox{in}\ (0,\infty),\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0pt\Phi\in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega).\end{array}\right.

Moreover, we shall require the further technical assumptions

(1.23) (fχ)′>0,on[0,∞)\left(\frac{f}{\chi}\right)^{\prime}>0,\quad\mbox{on}\ [0,\infty)
(1.24) (fχ)′′≤0,on[0,∞)\left(\frac{f}{\chi}\right)^{\prime\prime}\leq 0,\quad\mbox{on}\ [0,\infty)

and

(1.25) (χ⋅f)′≥0,on[0,∞).\left(\chi\cdot f\right)^{\prime}\geq 0,\quad\mbox{on}\ [0,\infty).

Our main result reads as follows.

Theorem 1.1.

Let Ω⊂ℝ3\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{3} be a bounded convex domain with smooth boundary and κ∈ℝ\kappa\in\mathbb{R}. Suppose that the assumptions (1)-(1.25) hold. Then there exists at least one global weak solution (in the sense of Definition 6.1 below) of (1)-(1.12) such that

nm2∈Ll​o​c2​([0,∞),W1,2​(Ω))andc14∈Ll​o​c4​([0,∞),W1,4​(Ω)).n^{\frac{m}{2}}\in L_{loc}^{2}([0,\infty);W^{1,2}(\Omega))\quad\mbox{and}\quad c^{\frac{1}{4}}\in L_{loc}^{4}([0,\infty);W^{1,4}(\Omega)).
Remark 1.1.

(i) If the diffusion function D⁡(u)≡1D(u)\equiv 1 in (1), this is consistent with the result of [29].

(ii) Theorem 1.1 shows that the model (1)-(1.12) possesses global weak solution even when the diffusion effect is rather mild. However, we have to leave open here whether the lower bound of diffusion exponent m=23m=\frac{2}{3} is optimal to guarantee global weak solvability.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we introduce a family of regularized problems and give some preliminary properties. Based on an energy-type inequality, a priori estimates are given in Section 3. Section 4 is devoted to showing the global existence of the regularized problems. In Section 5, we further establish some ε\varepsilon-independent estimates. Finally, we give the proof of the main result in Section 6.

2. Regularized problem

Our intention is to construct a global weak solution as the limit of smooth solutions of appropriately regularized problems. According to the idea from [29] (see also [20]), let us first consider the approximate problems
